sourceNote: Selective DGT editorial notes for Hebrews.

1:3: χαρακτήρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως describes the Son as the exact imprint of God’s underlying reality or being. DGT uses “exact imprint of his being” rather than importing later technical Trinitarian terminology into the verse.
1:8: The quotation addresses the Son with the words Ὁ θρόνος σου ὁ θεός. DGT renders this naturally as “Your throne, O God,” following the vocative sense of the quotation.
2:9: SBLGNT reads χάριτι θεοῦ, “by the grace of God.” A well-known variant reads χωρὶς θεοῦ, “apart from God.” DGT follows its displayed SBLGNT base text.
3:6: The warning clause is conditional: “if indeed we hold firmly…” DGT preserves that force rather than turning the statement into an unconditional description.
4:8: Ἰησοῦς is the Greek form used for both Jesus and Joshua. Here the reference is to Joshua son of Nun, so DGT translates the name as “Joshua.”
4:12: “Word of God” (ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ) can be read in relation to God’s spoken word in the preceding argument; DGT does not identify it specifically with Scripture or with Christ beyond what the verse itself says.
5:7: εἰσακουσθεὶς ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβείας can mean “heard because of his reverence/reverent submission.” DGT uses that sense while leaving open how the answer relates to Jesus’ death and resurrection.
6:4: Hebrews 6:4–6 describes people who were enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, became sharers in the Holy Spirit, and then fell away. DGT keeps the participles and warning force explicit rather than weakening them into merely apparent participation.
6:6: παραπεσόντας means “having fallen away.” The construction links this with the preceding participles and the impossibility of renewing such people again to repentance while they recrucify and publicly shame the Son of God.
7:3: Hebrews describes Melchizedek as “without father, without mother, without genealogy” within the scriptural presentation. DGT does not turn this into a claim about his literal biological origin.
7:25: εἰς τὸ παντελές can mean completely or forever. DGT uses “save completely,” while the following clause emphasizes Christ’s continuing life and intercession.
8:13: By calling the covenant “new,” Hebrews says the first has been made old and is near disappearance. DGT retains that temporal language directly.
9:4: The Greek θυμιατήριον can refer to an incense altar or censer. DGT uses “golden altar of incense”; the verse’s relationship to the Old Testament tabernacle layout is debated.
9:15: διαθήκη can mean covenant and, in some contexts, testament. Hebrews 9:16–17 exploits language associated with death and inheritance. DGT keeps “covenant” throughout so the argument’s wordplay remains visible rather than switching English terms midstream.
10:10: ἐφάπαξ means once for all. DGT keeps this emphatic finality in the statement about Christ’s bodily offering.
10:26: The participle is present and deliberate: “if we go on sinning deliberately.” DGT avoids reducing the warning either to a single isolated sin or to a vague hypothetical.
10:29: The person described has been “sanctified” by the blood of the covenant (ἐν ᾧ ἡγιάσθη). DGT leaves the referent and theological implications explicit rather than explaining them away.
11:1: ὑπόστασις can mean assurance, substance, or underlying reality; ἔλεγχος can mean conviction or proof. DGT uses “assurance” and “conviction,” while the Greek terms carry a broader semantic range.
11:11: The Greek grammar can be read with Sarah as the subject receiving power for conception, though the phrase is difficult. DGT follows that reading.
11:26: Hebrews says Moses considered “the reproach of Christ” greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures. DGT retains “Christ” rather than paraphrasing it as merely “the reproach borne for God’s people.”
12:15: The “root of bitterness” echoes Deuteronomy 29:18 and refers to a poisonous source of apostasy or defilement, not merely an individual feeling of resentment.
12:17: The pronoun in “he sought it with tears” most naturally refers to the blessing, not necessarily to repentance itself. DGT leaves the sentence close to the Greek so the distinction remains visible.
13:10: “We have an altar” is stated without explicit identification of the altar. DGT leaves the metaphor uninterpreted rather than specifying Eucharist, cross, or another referent.
13:22: The author calls Hebrews a “word of encouragement” and says it was written “briefly,” an interesting self-description for a rhetorically elaborate work.
